paragraphs.heading: Breaking food down
paragraphs.text: The human digestive system is the gastrointestinal tract, or GI tract, together with helper organs: the tongue, salivary glands, pancreas, liver and gallbladder. Its job is to break food into smaller and smaller parts until the body can absorb them and put them to use. The GI tract is the largest structure in the system, running from the mouth to the anus over a distance of about nine metres.

paragraphs.heading: Stage one, the cephalic phase
paragraphs.text: Digestion runs in three stages: the cephalic, gastric and intestinal phases. The cephalic phase begins when the sight and smell of food prompt the gastric glands to secrete. It carries on in the mouth, where chewing breaks food apart and enzymes in saliva, such as amylase and lingual lipase, start breaking it down chemically. Chewing also mixes food with saliva into a lump called a food bolus, which is swallowed down the esophagus into the stomach.

paragraphs.heading: Stage two, the stomach
paragraphs.text: In the gastric phase, the stomach mixes food with gastric juice and keeps breaking it down until it moves on to the duodenum, the first part of the small intestine. Millions of gastric glands embedded in the stomach's mucosa make this juice. Gastric juice, with its acid, and the mucus the stomach produces are both essential for digestion to continue. Digestion is also helped by peristalsis, rhythmic muscle contractions that start in the esophagus and carry on along the stomach and the rest of the tract.

paragraphs.heading: Stage three, the intestines
paragraphs.text: In the intestinal phase, the partly digested food is mixed with digestive enzymes from the pancreas, which completes digestion. Most of the digestion of food happens in the small intestine, which also absorbs water and nutrients into the bloodstream. It is the longest part of the GI tract but narrower than the large intestine. The large intestine takes back more water and electrolytes and stores the leftover waste, the feces, until it is expelled through the anus.

paragraphs.heading: Where it all starts
paragraphs.text: The mouth is the first part of the upper GI tract, and its salivary glands, teeth and tongue begin the first steps of digestion. It has two regions: the vestibule, between the teeth, lips and cheeks, and the oral cavity proper, which is the rest. Most of the mouth is lined with oral mucosa, a membrane that makes a lubricating mucus. The main part of mucus is a glycoprotein called mucin, and the mucin made in the mouth protects strongly against tooth decay.

paragraphs.heading: The roof of the mouth
paragraphs.text: The roof of the mouth, the palate, separates the oral cavity from the nasal cavity. At the front it is hard, since the mucosa there covers a plate of bone. At the back it is softer and more pliable, built from muscle and connective tissue, and it moves when we swallow food and liquids. This soft palate ends at the uvula. The hard front lets us press on food while eating and still keep the nasal passage clear.
